classification.difficultyReason: Connect equal reflection angles with supplementary and vertically opposite angles across two triangles, then generalise the numerical angle chase to show that y cancels and the elevation is 2x. The supplied diagram, reflection rule and preceding numerical cases scaffold this connection.

content.prompt: Suppose that the two mirrors are no longer parallel. The angle measured by the sextant is the angle between the two mirrors ($\angle ADB$ in this diagram).

spec.description: Two nonparallel mirrors with double-reflected light, object, horizon through B and C, dashed mirror extensions meeting at D, dashed incoming-ray extension AC, four reflection arcs and curved annotations pointing to C and D. Ordinary source-blue marks become black; construction extensions retain standard red. Coordinates establish an illustrative configuration and are not numerical givens.
spec.mathematics: The incident and reflected rays make equal angles with each mirror. AD and BD extend the mirrors; O, A and C are collinear. The angle of elevation is ACB, and the sextant measures ADB.
spec.answerVisibility: All displayed geometry is supplied; no numerical answers appear.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the angle of elevation, given that $\angle CBD=70^\circ$ and $\angle ADB=25^\circ$.

answer.worked:
Equal reflection angles at $B$ give
$$\begin{align*}\angle ABC&=180^\circ-2(70^\circ)\\\angle ABC&=40^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Since $BC$ lies inside $\angle ABD$, $\angle ABD=40^\circ+70^\circ=110^\circ$. In $\triangle ABD$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle DAB&=180^\circ-110^\circ-25^\circ\\\angle DAB&=45^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Reflection at $A$ and vertically opposite angles give $\angle DAC=45^\circ$, so $\angle BAC=90^\circ$. In $\triangle ABC$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle ACB&=180^\circ-90^\circ-40^\circ\\\angle ACB&=50^\circ.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the angle of elevation, given that $\angle CBD=64^\circ$ and $\angle ADB=39^\circ$.

answer.worked:
Equal reflection angles at $B$ give
$$\begin{align*}\angle ABC&=180^\circ-2(64^\circ)\\\angle ABC&=52^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Thus $\angle ABD=52^\circ+64^\circ=116^\circ$. In $\triangle ABD$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle DAB&=180^\circ-116^\circ-39^\circ\\\angle DAB&=25^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Reflection at $A$ and vertically opposite angles give $\angle DAC=25^\circ$, so $\angle BAC=50^\circ$. In $\triangle ABC$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle ACB&=180^\circ-50^\circ-52^\circ\\\angle ACB&=78^\circ.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: By investigating other values of $\angle CBD$ and $\angle ADB$, can you guess a connection between the angle measured on the sextant and the angle of elevation?

answer.short: The angle of elevation is twice the angle measured by the sextant.
answer.worked:
For example, take $\angle CBD=65^\circ$ and $\angle ADB=20^\circ$. Reflection gives $\angle ABC=50^\circ$ and $\angle ABD=115^\circ$. Triangle $ABD$ then gives $\angle DAB=45^\circ$, so reflection at $A$ gives $\angle BAC=90^\circ$. Hence $\angle ACB=40^\circ$.

With $\angle CBD=75^\circ$ and $\angle ADB=30^\circ$, the same method gives $\angle ABC=30^\circ$, $\angle ABD=105^\circ$, $\angle DAB=45^\circ$, $\angle BAC=90^\circ$ and $\angle ACB=60^\circ$.

These cases suggest that the angle of elevation is twice the angle measured by the sextant.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find the angle of elevation if $\angle CBD=y^\circ$ and $\angle ADB=x^\circ$.

answer.short:
$(2x)^\circ$.

Use equal reflection angles and the angle sums of triangles $ABD$ and $ABC$.
answer.worked:
Reflection at $B$ gives $\angle ABC=(180-2y)^\circ$. Thus
$$\begin{align*}\angle ABD&=(180-2y+y)^\circ\\\angle ABD&=(180-y)^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Using the angle sum of $\triangle ABD$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle DAB&=\bigl(180-(180-y)-x\bigr)^\circ\\\angle DAB&=(y-x)^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Reflection at $A$ and vertically opposite angles give $\angle DAC=(y-x)^\circ$, so $\angle BAC=2(y-x)^\circ$. Using the angle sum of $\triangle ABC$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle ACB&=\bigl(180-(180-2y)-2(y-x)\bigr)^\circ\\\angle ACB&=(2x)^\circ.\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: Does this general result agree with your conjecture of part c?

answer.worked: Yes. Part d gives an angle of elevation of $(2x)^\circ$ when the sextant measures $x^\circ$, confirming the conjecture in part c.
